segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a series dedicated to one of the greatest novels in the English language.
Over the course of this series, we'll be reading Dickens' masterwork closely — passage by passage, character by character, idea by idea.
We begin today where the novel itself begins: in fog.
Fog over the Thames, fog in the courts of Chancery, fog — as we'll discover — that gets into everything and everyone.
Joining me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel, each bringing a very different lens.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don, a lifelong Dickens scholar, and someone who believes the novel's true power lies in its moral imagination — in character, conscience, and the testing of the human soul.
He is, I should say, deeply suspicious of what he calls politicised readings — and not afraid to say so.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer, the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than almost anyone alive.
He comes to the novel as a performer — listening for the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments Dickens wrote for the voice rather than the eye.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since.
She reads for the experience of the prose — what's funny, what's moving, what makes you stop and re-read a sentence.
Let's begin with the novel's opening world: London, Chancery, and the extraordinary reach of both.
The very first thing Dickens does in this novel — before character, before plot — is establish a world saturated in obstruction.
The fog, the mud, the court of Chancery — they are not separate phenomena.
They are one atmosphere.
And it is into this atmosphere that Dickens introduces, quite brilliantly, the figure of Jarndyce himself — who describes the ruin that Chancery leaves in its wake.
He gives us a street — a real London street — consumed by the suit.

"It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door — and every door might be death's door — turning stagnant green."
Every door might be death's door.
That parenthetical lands like a quiet toll of a bell.
This is not mere social commentary — this is the gothic imagination at full power.
What strikes me every time I read that passage aloud is how physical it is — you can hear the shutters coming off their hinges.
Dickens didn't write for the study — he wrote for the voice, and that sentence is built to be performed.
Each clause adds one more detail of collapse — it's cumulative, almost musical.
And then there's Tulkinghorn — a completely different kind of fog, a human fog.
Dickens gives us this wonderful description of the man's movements between Chesney Wold and his London chambers.
"He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields."
He melts in and out of places.
That's Dickens' word — melts.
A man who moves like something dissolving into the furniture — how can you not find that sinister and magnificent in equal measure?
I take Oliver's point about the voice entirely — though I'd add that the cumulative syntax also has a precise moral weight.
Jarndyce ends that passage with a line I find almost unbearable in its simplicity.
"These are the Great Seal's impressions, my dear, all over England — the children know them!"
The children know them.
That exclamation is not triumphant — it is devastating.
Chancery's ruin is so pervasive, so ordinary, that the youngest members of society simply recognise it as part of the landscape.
That is where Dickens' moral imagination operates at its most devastating — not in the polemical passages, but in the small, quiet observations.
What I love about both those passages is how different they are in texture — and yet they're both about the same invisible force.
Jarndyce's street is all surface — visible decay, things falling apart that you can touch and smell.
Tulkinghorn's mystery is precisely the opposite — nothing is visible at all.
But Dickens also gives us something else entirely — the interior of Bleak House itself.
And this is what I keep coming back to on every re-reading: the warmth of that house is not sentimental.
It's earned — it's specific.
Esther describes her first impressions with this extraordinary trailing sentence — let me read it.

"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House."
That phrase — hospitable jingle — is almost ridiculous, and yet it's completely perfect.
You hear the warmth before you see it.
"Hospitable jingle" — I've recorded that sentence three times now and I still have to slow down for that phrase.
Because there's a temptation to sweep through it — it's such a long, rolling sentence — but if you rush that phrase you lose the whole joke.
There's laughter in that sentence.
And joy — genuine joy.
I think this is why Bleak House is so extraordinary — it holds bleakness and joy simultaneously, and makes both feel true.
And yet one must not overlook what Dickens places in deliberate counterpoint to all of that warmth.
There is another world in this novel — the world of Chesney Wold, of the Dedlock interest, of Sir Leicester himself.
And Dickens describes that world with a comic precision that is, frankly, surgical.
"He has a general opinion that the world might get on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks."
Done up.
It is gloriously vulgar, in the very best sense — a slang phrase intruding into baronial self-importance.
Dickens' comic gift is not separate from his moral imagination — it is the instrument of it.
That phrase — done up without Dedlocks — does seem to sum up an entire class in four words.
And in a way, we've already arrived at the novel's central tension: between those who believe the world depends on them, and those quietly holding it together.

In our next segment, we'll turn to the court of Chancery itself — and to the novel's extraordinary double narration, which puts an institution and a young woman into conversation across two hundred years.

segments.title: A Gentleman's Fall: Richard's Descent into the Chancery Trap

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart, chapter by chapter, passage by passage, to see what's really working inside it.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most quietly devastating stories: the slow ruin of Richard Carstone.
A young man of genuine charm and ability, consumed — not suddenly but by degrees — by a lawsuit that was never going to save him.
With me, as ever, are three readers I trust completely with this material.
Sir Edmund Leigh, the Oxford don and moral critic, who believes Richard's tragedy is finally a story about character, not about institutions.
Oliver Trevelyan, actor and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any living person, who hears the novel the way Dickens intended — performed, out loud, for an audience.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted Dickens reader, who knows this novel from the inside and feels every page of it.
Edmund, let's begin with you — and with Dickens' portrait of the world Richard inhabits: a world of ancient houses, old money, and the comfortable illusions of permanence.
Thank you.
It is worth pausing on the world that surrounds Richard before we consider the man himself — because Dickens is quite deliberate in the contrast he establishes.
There is, on one side, a portrait of England as rooted permanence — Chesney Wold, the ancient house, Sir Leicester's immovable self-satisfaction.
Dickens gives us this passage, which I confess I find rather beautiful despite its satirical intent.
"Where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the fern and leaves of a hundred years."
The language is doing two things simultaneously, which is Dickens at his most sophisticated.
It mocks Sir Leicester's complacency — that self-opposing repose — and yet the prose itself carries genuine affection for the English landscape it describes.
Richard has no such rootedness. He has expectations, and a lawsuit, and very little else.
Edmund puts his finger on something important there, and I want to push it a little further from the performing side.
Because when you read Bleak House aloud — and I mean really aloud, finding the voices — you notice that Richard never quite has his own voice in the way that, say, Jarndyce does.
Jarndyce has weight, has texture, has the marvellous comic music of a man who genuinely knows himself.
There's that wonderful moment — Chapter Nine — where Jarndyce describes Boythorn to the young people, and listen to the sheer delight in it.

"There! I tell you no more of him beforehand. You must not be surprised to see him take me under his protection, for he has never forgotten that I was a low boy at school and that our friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant's teeth out — he says six — before breakfast."
Now that is a man who has lived, who has been knocked about and loved it, and who tells a story with perfect timing.
Richard cannot do that. Richard's voice is always reaching for something — restless, unfocused — and that restlessness is the tragedy made audible.
What Oliver says about Richard's voice resonates with me deeply, because it connects to the most troubling passage I keep returning to in this section.
It's a passage from Esther — characteristically indirect, characteristically painful — where she reflects on what Woodcourt has noticed about Richard.
And she gives us this, which I think is one of the most quietly devastating sentences in the entire novel.
"It revived a fear I had had before that my dear girl's little property would be absorbed by Mr. Vholes and that Richard's justification to himself would be sincerely this."
Sincerely this.
Those two words do so much work. It's not that Richard is a liar or even consciously selfish.
It's that he has genuinely convinced himself — and that is so much worse.
Esther sees it. Woodcourt sees it. Ada, who loves him most, cannot bear to see it.
Caroline is absolutely right, and I think this is where I must respectfully part company with those who read Richard simply as a victim of Chancery.
Chancery is the occasion of Richard's ruin, but not its cause.
The cause is a weakness of will — a constitutional inability to commit to anything that does not promise a miraculous resolution.
Burke would have recognised it immediately: the man who mistakes expectation for inheritance, and hope for plan.
Dickens shows us the full irony in the Dedlock passages, where we see what genuine — if comically inflated — rootedness looks like by contrast.
Sir Leicester is absurd, yes — Dickens does not let him entirely off — but he is at least coherent.
Richard is incoherent because he has substituted the lawsuit for a self.
I love that — substituted the lawsuit for a self. That's exactly it.
And what makes it so effective on the page — and on the stage, or wherever Dickens is performed — is that Richard is genuinely likeable.
Dickens gives him the charm without the backbone. You want to shake him and embrace him in equal measure.
Think of Jarndyce's description of Boythorn again — that life force, that glorious excess of vitality.
Jarndyce says of Boythorn: "His language is as sounding as his voice. He is always in extremes, perpetually in the superlative degree."
Richard is also in extremes, but his extremes are of hope and despair, not of magnificent energy.
Boythorn's excess is life. Richard's excess is erosion. Same superlative degree, opposite direction.
And what I find unbearable — in the best possible reading sense — is that Esther watches all of this and cannot intervene.
The structure of the narration enacts the tragedy. She knows, Woodcourt knows, and the knowledge is useless.
There's that small, devastating phrase — "the shade was still between me and my darling" — which Dickens drops at the end of the passage almost without ceremony.
Ada has chosen Richard, and that choice has placed her beyond Esther's reach.
The shade. Not a wall, not a quarrel — a shade.
That is Dickens knowing exactly what word to choose, and placing it where the light is going out.
The shade. That image will stay with me.
Richard consumed by the suit, Ada lost behind the shade, and Esther watching both — Dickens has drawn the trap with extraordinary precision.
In our next segment, we'll look at the mechanisms of that trap more closely — the lawyers, the system, and the question of who, if anyone, is truly to blame.

segments.title: The Veiled Woman: Secrets, Social Position, and Lady Dedlock's Unraveling

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' great dark cathedral of a novel and opens every door.
Today we are deep inside one of the novel's most electrifying dramatic engines: Lady Dedlock herself.
A woman of perfect surface and shattering secret — aristocrat, mother, fugitive from her own past.
With me to unpick the veils are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, Dickens moralist, and a man who believes the fog is a literary device and not a manifesto.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any living soul — who hears what the rest of us only read.
And Caroline Woodcourt — book critic, five-time reader of Bleak House, and the person in this room most likely to stop mid-sentence to marvel at a single phrase.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because Dickens introduces Lady Dedlock in Chapter Two, and the way he does it is, I think, almost perverse in its brilliance.
It is perverse, yes — and I mean that as the highest compliment.
He spends something like four hundred words on the weather in Lincolnshire before he lets Lady Dedlock exist on the page as a person.
The rain, the soaked deer, the flagstones, the drip, drip, drip — all of that arrives first.
And then he gives us this line, which I find almost unbearably beautiful in its economy.
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
That is Lady Dedlock's world — rendered entirely in tones of grey and black, with no warmth, no colour, no entry in.
And the sentence doesn't describe her directly — it describes her view — which is precisely the point.
We are looking at what she sees, not at her — and yet we understand her completely.
Caroline is right about the economy — though I would add that Dickens is doing something even more classical there.
He is giving us pathetic fallacy — and doing it with almost Augustan control.
The landscape is not a metaphor for social decay, as some would insist on reading it — it is a moral mirror for a particular soul.
And what cuts deepest in that passage, I think, is the aside.
Dickens tells us Lady Dedlock is childless — in parentheses, as a matter of cold fact — and then immediately shows her watching a child run out to meet its father.
And what is her response to that small, ordinary scene of domestic joy?
She is — to use her own word — "bored to death."
That is not the language of boredom — that is the language of a woman being destroyed from within by something she will not name.
Edmund, yes — but I want to stop at that parenthesis, because when you're performing this, that single word "childless" is everything.
Dickens drops it in with a kind of brutal casualness — as if it were merely biographical detail — and then the whole passage ignites.
Now — moving to Tulkinghorn, because he is the engine of destruction in this novel, and Dickens introduces him with a passage that I confess I could read until I die.
Here is the thing about Tulkinghorn — he arrives always at this exactly measured pace, and Dickens catches it:
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb. Every crease. The man is secrets, all the way down.
And then Dickens asks the question he will never quite answer:
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great, or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells, is his personal secret."
He is his own client. That is perhaps the coldest line in the novel.
"He is his own client" — I've never read that and not felt a small chill.
Because every other character in this novel is entangled, exposed, legible to someone — but Tulkinghorn is hermetically sealed.
Which makes what he does with Lady Dedlock's portrait so devastating.
He stands before it — this image of perfect aristocratic composure — and his verdict is:
"A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character."
It wants force of character. Said of a woman who is holding herself together by sheer, ferocious will.
The cruelty of that is almost architectural — and the worst part is, he knows exactly what he is doing.
Caroline has put her finger on something essential about the power dynamic here.
Tulkinghorn is not cruel in the vulgar, melodramatic sense — he is methodical.
And Dickens captures that methodical menace in the passage where he observes Lady Dedlock after she has received his threat:
"This woman thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view — is a study."
A study. Not a human being in extremis — a problem to be examined.
That is his evil — and Dickens renders it with such restraint that it lands harder than any operatic villainy could.
And notice what she does in response — she drinks water with a steady hand, she reclines, she shades her face.
There is nothing, Dickens tells us, in her manner to express weakness or excite compassion.
That is not weakness — that is a kind of magnificent, terrible courage.
Magnificent and terrible — yes, that's exactly the register.
And you know, the thing that always strikes me when I'm performing these passages — Dickens writes Lady Dedlock's composure as a kind of performance in itself.
She is always being watched — by Tulkinghorn, by the fashionable world, by the omniscient narrator — and she knows it.
Which is what makes the scene with Esther in the wood so extraordinary — because there, for once, the performance cracks.
Esther sees her coming through the trees at an unusual pace — and Caroline, you've written beautifully about this moment.
That passage — I have to be honest — makes me catch my breath every time.
Esther is sitting at her favourite spot, Charley is gathering violets — there's this quality of pastoral stillness — and then:
"By little and little it revealed itself to be a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's."
Those three degrees of recognition — woman, lady, Lady Dedlock — that is a masterclass in sentence rhythm.
Esther doesn't know yet — consciously — who she is looking at or why her heart should quicken.
But Dickens does — and the reader does, if they're paying attention — and that layered knowledge is what makes this scene so unbearably suspenseful.
And Lady Dedlock is coming quickly — with a much quicker step than was usual with her.
That small detail — the broken composure in her stride — is the most human thing Dickens has allowed her, up to this point.
What Caroline describes — the layers of knowledge between narrator, character, and reader — is, to my mind, the novel's supreme technical achievement.
Dickens is conducting three conversations simultaneously: with Esther's innocence, with the reader's suspicion, and with his own irony.
And Lady Dedlock sits at the centre of all three — a woman who has been reduced, by years of concealment, to pure performance.
Until the performance fails. Until she walks too quickly through a wood.
"Walks too quickly through a wood" — Edmund, that is a phrase I shall be living with for some time.
What we've uncovered today is just how completely Dickens constructed Lady Dedlock from the outside in — landscape, portrait, footstep — before he allowed her a single unguarded moment.
And the terrible irony is that the one man who truly reads her — Tulkinghorn — reads her only to use what he finds.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has made me want to go back to page one.
We'll be back shortly with the next segment — and if you think Lady Dedlock's secrets are heavy, wait until we turn to Chancery.

segments.title: Street Crossing and Social Poison: Jo's Tragedy as Critique

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great fog-bound novel apart, passage by passage, to see what's really inside.
I'm your host, and today we're examining one of the novel's most devastating threads — the tragedy of Jo, the crossing-sweeper, and what Dickens makes it mean.
Jo is a child who knows nothing — not his own age, not how to read, not why he is perpetually moved on — and Dickens turns that ignorance into an indictment.
To help us unpack all of this, I'm joined by three extraordinary readers of the novel.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a novel about character — about will, about goodness, about what individual conscience can and cannot do against the crush of circumstance.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than any living person — he hears the prose as performance, and he brings that performer's instinct to every passage we discuss.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens — she reads for the verbal music, for the emotional truth, and she is wonderfully alert to what the text actually does on the page.
Edmund, let's begin with you — because the passages we have before us today aren't only about Jo.
They bring in Sir Leicester, Skimpole, Woodcourt, even Miss Flite — and that constellation of characters seems to me to be doing something deliberate.
What is Dickens assembling here, and why does it matter?
Thank you — and what Dickens is assembling, I think, is a kind of moral cartography.
He places figures from entirely different social strata into proximity — and the juxtaposition itself is the argument.
Consider Sir Leicester Dedlock in the passage before us — a man of immense dignity and, on his own terms, genuine honour.
And yet his concern — his pain, mark you, his personal pain — is that Harold Skimpole was prevented from viewing the Chesney Wold pictures at sufficient leisure.
Dickens gives us the scene with perfect comic precision — listen to what Sir Leicester actually says:

"I assure you, sir, it has given—me—pain—to learn from the housekeeper at Chesney Wold that a gentleman who was in your company in that part of the county... was likewise deterred by some such cause from examining the family pictures with that leisure, that attention, that care, which he might have desired to bestow upon them."
Those dashes around the word 'pain' — Dickens is parodying pomposity, certainly — but he is also showing us something darker.
Sir Leicester's capacity for indignation — genuine, heartfelt indignation — is fully engaged by an inconvenience to an aesthete's tour of his gallery.
While Jo sweeps crossings and dies in a back room having never been permitted to understand why.
Edmund, you're absolutely right about those dashes — and when you perform that passage, they are irresistible.
Dickens has written the comic timing directly into the punctuation — which is something he does nowhere else quite so brilliantly.
But there's something else — Skimpole's name.
Sir Leicester mangles it — Hirrold, Herald, Harold, Skampling, Skumpling — and what could have been a throwaway gag is actually Dickens telling us something devastating.
This man cannot even be bothered to remember the name of the person on whose behalf he is registering pain.
And Skimpole, let us not forget, is himself a man who trades on the kindness of others while caring for precisely no one.
The pairing of these two — the aristocrat and the parasite — is Dickens at his most structurally cunning.
Two men whose feelings are entirely self-referential, framed by a novel full of people who cannot afford feelings at all.
What strikes me — and Oliver, you've touched on it — is that Dickens never lets the comedy neutralise the cruelty.
They coexist, and that's profoundly uncomfortable.
And then you turn to a passage like Richard's greeting to Woodcourt — and the emotional register shifts entirely.
Richard says, and I love this line so much:
"Woodcourt, my dear fellow — you come upon my vision like a ghost."
And you think — oh, Richard.
He means it as warmth and surprise — but Dickens has loaded the word 'ghost' with the knowledge of what Richard is becoming.
Richard himself is already a kind of ghost — consumed by Jarndyce and Jarndyce, fading from the inside out.
And Woodcourt — steady, real, present — comes upon him like something from another world entirely.
Caroline has identified something I think is central to the novel's moral architecture — and I'd put it this way.
Woodcourt functions in the novel as a figure of genuine, active goodness — not sentimental goodness, not passive goodness, but the kind that costs something.
And it is precisely this that makes the contrast with figures like Skimpole — and like the Chancery system itself — so morally legible.
Miss Flite's gratitude to Woodcourt, which Esther notes — her affection and her warmth — is not merely touching.
Esther says of her:
"Her gratitude to you, Mr. Woodcourt, is delightful. She is a most affectionate creature, as I have reason to say."
'As I have reason to say' — that quiet clause does a great deal of work.
Esther, who narrates half this novel in a state of relentless self-abnegation, is here allowing herself — very briefly — to acknowledge that Woodcourt has also been kind to her.
These are the people who are not moved on.
Edmund, 'moved on' — that's the phrase at the black heart of this novel, isn't it.
Jo is perpetually told to move on — by the police, by the law, by anyone with the authority to say so — and he never understands why.
And one of the most extraordinary things about performing that — about reading Jo's scenes aloud — is that the prose does something very strange.
The sentences get shorter.
Dickens narrows the vocabulary, compresses the syntax — it's as though the prose itself is enacting Jo's limited horizon.
And then set against that — Sir Leicester producing his card and reading, with enormous gravity, 'Mr. Hirrold — Herald — Harold — Skampling — Skumpling.'
You could play that scene for five minutes and not exhaust the comedy.
But the comedy is always doing something else underneath.
Oliver, that word 'underneath' — that's where I find myself most often in this novel.
There's the surface — the comedy, the grotesques, the magnificent pomposity of Sir Leicester — and then there's the weight beneath it.
And what I keep returning to is the moment when Jarndyce asks Esther — quite gently, almost tenderly — what she makes of Mrs. Woodcourt.
He says — and there's something so carefully watchful in this:
"He has made his protest, and Dame Durden has made hers, and there is nothing more to be said about it. Now I come to Mrs. Woodcourt. How do you like her, my dear?"
'How do you like her, my dear' — Jarndyce is protecting Esther even in the asking.
He has read her heart — he has always read her heart — and he is steering away from what would pain her, toward something manageable.
That quality of guardian-ship — of watching over someone without letting them see you watching — is, to me, one of Dickens's most quietly radical acts of characterisation.
That's a beautiful place to pause — guardianship, watchfulness, and the very different ways this novel distributes care and indifference across its social world.

We have the self-regarding pain of Sir Leicester, the uncomprehending misery of Jo, and the quiet, persistent attention of Woodcourt and Jarndyce — and Dickens asks us to feel the difference in our bones.
We'll be back shortly to consider how the fog that opens this novel — that famous, magnificent fog — reaches into all of these lives and what exactly Dickens intends by it.

segments.title: Comic Relief and Grotesquerie: Dickens' Darkly Comic Chorus

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's darker architecture — the fog, the Court, the slow grind of Chancery.
But Bleak House is also ferociously funny.
Dickens populates the novel with grotesques — figures so exaggerated they become almost mythological.
The comedy is never merely decorative; it bites.
To dig into this, I want to start with Oliver Trevelyan, who has lived inside Dickens' comic rhythms more intimately than perhaps anyone.
Oliver, there's a passage in Chapter Thirty-Nine — the court around Krook's old shop, convulsed by rumour and greed — that I think shows Dickens at his most carnivalesque.
Oh, that passage is a gift.
It's Dickens writing for the crowd in both senses — the fictional crowd outside Krook's shop, and his actual readers, who he knew would roar.
The whole court has gone delirious with speculation about hidden treasure.
And Dickens gives us this magnificent opening line — let me read it.
"Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop."
A Fortunatus' purse — bottomless, self-replenishing.
The gossip never empties, it only multiplies.
That single classical allusion does so much work.
And then he piles it on — the court imagining guineas pouring out of tea-pots, Bank of England notes stuffed into old mattresses.
The collective fantasy of the poor is rendered with enormous comic sympathy.
These people have nothing — and so they dream of everything, with magnificent specificity.
Then comes the music hall — Little Swills on the Harmonic nights, Miss M. Melvilleson pointing her chin knowingly next door.
The Sol Tavern incorporates the Smallweed search into its entertainment programme — this is a community making art out of obsession.
It's absurd and it's touching and it's completely alive.
What strikes me in that passage is the word 'maddened.'
'What those treasures are they keep so secret that the court is maddened.'
Dickens treats the court as a single organism with a single fever.
It's like watching a flock of birds turn together — there's no individual decision, just collective hysteria rendered as comedy.
And then the comedy shades into something slightly darker.
These people will discover nothing, as Dickens tells us plainly.
The laughter has a hollow bottom.
Miss Woodcourt puts her finger on something essential.
Dickens' comedy in this novel is never merely escapist.
The laughter functions as a kind of moral audit — we laugh at the court's delusion precisely because we can see what those people cannot.
Johnson had a phrase for this — the comedy of vanity, which is only comic to those outside the vanity.
The court around Krook's shop is a study in collective self-deception, and Dickens renders it with the clarity of a natural philosopher observing a colony of ants.
That is his great gift — the capacity to observe human folly without losing human sympathy.
That combination — clarity and sympathy — seems equally at play when Dickens turns his comedy on the upper classes.
Oliver, you've also been thinking about that famous passage in Chapter Two — Lady Dedlock and the merchants who manage her so expertly.
The Gulliver passage — yes.
This is Dickens at his most Swift-like — the satire is impeccably polite and absolutely lethal.
Lady Dedlock believes she is entirely inscrutable.
Every dim little star orbiting her knows her inside out.
And then Dickens produces this image — let me read it exactly.
"Who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
The fashionable world as a fleet of tiny warships towed along by a giant who doesn't even notice he's doing it.
The comedy is in the scale — the enormous pretension of the Dedlock world reduced to something a child could carry.
One should note that Swift himself would have admired that particular deployment of the Gulliver image.
It inverts the original — in Swift, Gulliver is the giant among the Lilliputians.
Here, the tradespeople are Gulliver and the aristocracy are the diminished fleet.
Power has quietly migrated from the titled class to the commercial class — and the titled class has not noticed.
That is sharp social observation dressed as a classical joke.
What I love is Mr. Sladdery — the librarian who repeats 'my high connexion, sir' until it becomes a kind of incantation.
Dickens is doing something very precise with that repetition.
Each time Sladdery says 'my high connexion, sir,' the phrase deflates a little more.
And then the kicker — 'in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not exaggerate at all.'
That deadpan confirmation is the funniest possible ending to that sentence.
It's so dry it could ignite.
That comic precision — and we haven't yet mentioned one of the novel's great comic monsters: Harold Skimpole.
Edmund, I know you have strong views about where Skimpole sits in Dickens' moral universe.
Skimpole is one of the most carefully constructed villains in the English novel — and I use that word with full deliberation.
He presents as a charming child-man, airy and irresponsible, with a gift for making his selfishness sound like philosophy.
And Dickens gives us the formulation in Chapter Thirty-One that exposes the whole structure.

"What Harold Skimpole was, Harold Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the bargain."
'Sound philosophy' — what breathtaking impudence.
It is the philosophy of a man who has decided that moral effort is for other people, and has dressed that decision in aesthetic language.
Burke would have recognised him instantly — the man who converts irresponsibility into a creed.
Edmund is right that it's devastating, but I'd push back slightly on 'villain.'
Skimpole is genuinely funny — Dickens loves the performance of him, even as he damns him.
That passage where he raises his glass and imagines Jo becoming Lord Mayor, endowing the Summerson Almshouses — he's delighted by his own absurdity.
He 'absolutely chirped' — that's a word Dickens chose for a reason.
A chirping villain is something richer than a merely sinister one.
The comedy is the corruption — they are the same thing, inseparable.
And the comedy curdles beautifully as the novel progresses.
You start reading Skimpole with a kind of helpless delight — he is irresistible.
Then you remember Jo.
You remember what Skimpole's charming irresponsibility actually costs — in human lives, in the lives of the vulnerable.
That retrospective horror is a technique — Dickens is teaching you not to be seduced by elegant speech.
It's a moral education delivered via entertainment.
Miss Woodcourt's point connects to something Krook embodies differently — the comic that is simultaneously gothic.
There is a brief moment in Chapter Five — Esther watching Krook trace letters on the wall — that captures this perfectly.
The passage is almost deceptively spare.

"When I told him, he laughed. In the same odd way, yet with the same rapidity, he then produced singly, and rubbed out singly, the letters forming the words Bleak House. These, in some astonishment, I also read; and he laughed again."
Three sentences.
That laugh — repeated, unexplained — is the sound of the novel's own mystery looking at Esther.
Krook is comic in his shabbiness and grotesque in his knowledge — and Dickens holds both qualities in a single, unsettling 'he laughed again.'
Reading Krook aloud, that laugh is absolutely the moment you pause.
Not a comic laugh — something stranger, more private.
When I record Krook, I always make that second laugh slightly quieter than the first.
It suggests he's hearing something Esther can't — that the joke is hers, not his.
The text permits that reading, which is a sign of how fully imagined the character is.
The comedy that knows something the reader doesn't — and the comedy that teaches something the reader must learn.
These are the twin engines of Dickens' darkly comic chorus in Bleak House.
We'll pause here and return to look more closely at the novel's structure of surveillance — who watches whom in this world, and at what cost.

segments.title: Where the Threads Tangle: Connections Across Class and Fate

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens's great fog-bound novel apart, passage by passage, to see what it's really made of.

Today's segment is called 'Where the Threads Tangle' — and it concerns what I think is one of the novel's most quietly astonishing achievements: the way Dickens weaves together lives that have no business touching each other.

A dying street-sweeper. A guardian of almost saintly generosity. A society lawyer who serves the aristocracy with something darker than loyalty. A charming parasite who somehow escapes all moral reckoning.

With me as always are Sir Edmund Leigh — Oxford don and Dickens's most rigorous moral reader; Oliver Trevelyan — the man who has given voice to more Dickens characters than perhaps any living person; and Caroline Woodcourt — critic, close reader, and someone who has lived with this novel for decades.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because you've been given a passage I suspect you've been waiting to talk about.
You're right — and the reason I've been waiting is Phil Squod.
Phil Squod, who has a smoky gunpowder visage and one functional eyebrow and has absolutely no reason whatsoever to be nursing a dying boy — and yet there he is.
The passage opens on this extraordinary domestic scene — an armourer working at his little table in the corner while simultaneously keeping watch over Jo.
And the encouragement Phil offers — Dickens writes it so you can hear it — is this:
"Hold up, my boy! Hold up!"
Two words of command — the words you'd use on a horse, or a soldier — and somehow they're the most tender thing in the scene.
But it's what comes just after that stops me every time I record it.
"Both thinking, much, how strangely fate has entangled this rough outcast in the web of very different lives."
That word — entangled — is doing an enormous amount of work.
It's not joined, not connected — entangled: something that happened against the logic of the world, and can't now be undone.
Oliver is right to press on that word, and I'd push the observation slightly further.
The web Dickens invokes is not a social web — not Chancery, not the class system — it is, at its deepest, a moral web.
What binds Jarndyce to Jo, or Woodcourt to Jo, is not politics. It is the capacity for human sympathy acting against interest.
Consider what Dickens gives us in the trooper — George — who fills the doorway with his athletic figure.
And Dickens says he seems, from his superfluity of life and strength, to shed down temporary vigour upon Jo.
Superfluity of life — the excess of vitality in a healthy man becoming, almost physically, a gift to a dying one.
Burke wrote of the little platoons of society — the small loyalties that constitute genuine community. This room in George's shooting gallery is one of them.
What Edmund says about moral sympathy — yes, absolutely — but I want to stay with the texture of that scene for a moment.
Because what Dickens has done is gathered these men — Jarndyce, Woodcourt, George, Phil Squod — around a boy whom polite society has spent the entire novel telling to move on.
"Move on" — that's Jo's persistent instruction from authority. And here, everyone has stopped moving. Everyone has gathered.
The counterpoint to all that official dispersal is this quiet, makeshift family around a deathbed.
And Dickens earns that pathos — not with sentiment — but with Phil Squod's gunpowder face and his one raised eyebrow.
Caroline's pointed at something I feel very strongly as a performer — which is that the comic grotesque and the tragic are never far apart in Dickens.
Phil Squod is a figure from the absurdist comedy of the shooting gallery — and then he becomes a nurse.
Dickens doesn't explain the transformation. He doesn't justify it. He simply presents it as the most natural thing in the world.
Which brings me to a very different kind of character who also escapes ordinary moral explanation — though with considerably less virtue — Harold Skimpole.
Esther's narration of Skimpole is one of the great comic feats of the novel — partly because Esther herself doesn't quite know what to make of him.
She watches him speak of himself in the third person — as if Skimpole were someone else's problem — and writes:
"He was quite enchanting."
Three words — and they are both absolutely sincere and absolutely damning. That is Esther's genius as a narrator.
But the passage that really bites is what follows — Esther's honest admission of her own confusion.
"I was confused by not exactly understanding why he was free of them. That he was free of them, I scarcely doubted; he was so very clear about it himself."
That last clause — 'he was so very clear about it himself' — is the most perfectly placed comic sting in the entire chapter.
Skimpole is, I would argue, the most morally dangerous character in the novel — far more dangerous than Tulkinghorn.
Tulkinghorn is corrupt in a manner that society at least recognises as corruptible. Skimpole has invented an entire philosophy to justify his parasitism — and it is a charming one.
Dickens himself — and this is a biographical detail worth noting — drew Skimpole from a living original, and later expressed deep regret at how recognisable the portrait was.
But what Dickens captures, with frightening precision, is the way a person who refuses duty manages nonetheless to be beloved.
Esther sees through him — eventually — but her account of being charmed is as honest as anything in her narrative.
I think what makes Esther's confusion so affecting is that Dickens gives her full credit for it.
She doesn't pretend to have seen through Skimpole from the start. She admits she was confused and that his confidence in his own freedom was almost convincing.
That phrase — the duties and accountabilities of life — is Esther's moral vocabulary, and it's a rich one.
She lives by it. Skimpole lives against it. And the novel, with enormous patience, shows us why that matters.
And threading through all of this is a man who serves a very different set of accountabilities — Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Oliver, you have a passage on him too — and it's one of Dickens's great ironic portraits. What does it give us?
Tulkinghorn is a masterclass in what I think of as Dickens's negative portraiture — the art of describing someone entirely by what they withhold.
Listen to the list Dickens gives us. Rustily dressed. Close and dry in manner. Husky and low in voice.
Watchful behind a blind. Each phrase is a closed door.
And then Dickens twists the knife with the most perfectly balanced irony in the chapter:
"The peerage may have warmer worshippers and faithfuller believers than Mr. Tulkinghorn, after all, if everything were known."
If everything were known — four words that make Tulkinghorn more threatening than a hundred direct accusations could.
He doesn't serve the aristocracy out of reverence. He serves them out of something far colder. Power, perhaps. Or simply the pleasure of possession — the possession of secrets.
Oliver's reading is theatrically impeccable and I'd only add one thing.
That phrase 'spectacles in his hand, and their very case worn threadbare' — the threadbare case — is Dickens at his most concentrated.
Tulkinghorn is a man who has spent himself entirely in the service of others' affairs and retained nothing for himself — not warmth, not humanity, not even a decent spectacle-case.
The irony of the final sentence is not merely satirical. It is also, I think, a kind of pity.
I find it very hard to pity Tulkinghorn — but Edmund's point about that detail is exactly right.
Dickens makes him frightening through accumulation — the rustiness, the dryness, the hushed voice — it all adds up to someone who has chosen to become a cipher.
And then Jarndyce's speech to Mrs. Woodcourt — which I've been sitting with — does something entirely opposite.
Where Tulkinghorn hoards information as leverage, Jarndyce opens everything — lays Esther's history bare — as an act of love.
The passage where he confronts Mrs. Woodcourt about Esther's pedigree — I have to read it, because the rhythm of it is extraordinary:
"Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this — for I scorned to mince it — and tell me what is the true legitimacy."
'I scorned to mince it.' That one clause. That is Jarndyce's character in seven words.
Jarndyce is, I will always maintain, the moral centre of the novel — and that passage is the proof.
'What is the true legitimacy' — it is a question Dickens poses against an entire social order that would judge Esther by birth rather than character.
And crucially, Dickens does not make this a tirade. He gives it to a gentleman — speaking with the authority of a gentleman — which is, I think, the more subversive choice.
And Esther is receiving this account of herself in real time — hearing how thoroughly and how lovingly she has been defended in her absence.
Dickens has constructed the revelation beautifully — because Esther can't quite respond to it directly.
She can only write it down, for us, years later — and in doing so, she finally allows herself to receive the love that she's been deflecting throughout the entire novel.
And there it is — the web that Oliver named at the start of this segment, pulled taut.
Jo, Phil Squod, Tulkinghorn, Skimpole, Jarndyce, Esther — lives that have no business touching, all of them entangled by fate, and by Dickens's extraordinary structural intelligence.
We'll pick up the thread again shortly — after the break.

segments.title: Bleak House Unresolved: What Dickens' Ending Reveals and Withholds

utterances.text: We've arrived at the end — not just of our episode, but of the novel itself.
Bleak House closes, as it opens, in a state of irresolution — loose threads gathered but never quite tied.
For this final conversation, I want to ask each of our guests what the ending reveals — and perhaps more importantly, what it withholds.
Sir Edmund, you've been thinking about the moral architecture of the novel throughout — shall we begin with you?
Thank you. The question of what a novel's ending withholds is, I think, the most searching question one can put to a work of fiction.
And Bleak House, characteristically, withholds resolution precisely where it matters most — in the moral education of its characters.
Consider Jarndyce's counsel to Richard and Ada — one of the most quietly devastating moments in the entire novel.
He has watched everything — he has lived inside the ruin that Chancery makes of human hope.
And so when he speaks, he speaks with the full weight of experience that the novel has accumulated.
"I ask you wholly to relinquish, for the present, any tie but your relationship."
That word — wholly — carries an extraordinary burden.
Jarndyce is asking them to unmake a love in order to preserve a person.
And what's devastating — performatively, I mean — is how Dickens keeps Jarndyce's voice so level, so almost mild.
There's no melodrama in that speech, and yet it contains an absolute earthquake.
Dickens understood — better than almost anyone — that the most wounding lines are delivered quietly.
When I read it aloud, I always feel the temptation to push the emotion — and the text simply won't allow it.
The prose itself acts as a restraint on the performer.
Which is, I suppose, what great writing does — it tells you exactly how to deliver it, if you listen closely enough.
I keep returning to a much smaller moment — one that isn't devastating at all, on the surface.
Mrs. Woodcourt — Allan's mother — comes to stay at Bleak House, and Esther finds her almost uncomfortably confidential.
Dickens writes — and this is Esther's voice, so there's already a veil over the feeling —
"She took very kindly to me and was extremely confidential, so much so that sometimes she almost made me uncomfortable."
That "almost" is Esther all over — she can barely bring herself to name her own feelings, even to us.
And what Mrs. Woodcourt is being confidential about, of course, is her son — she's taking the measure of Esther.
So this cosy scene is actually teeming with suppressed hope and suppressed anxiety.
That's what the novel withholds — it never quite lets Esther be fully known, even by herself.
That observation about Esther's self-concealment strikes me as quite right — and it connects, I think, to the larger structural problem of the ending.
The omniscient narrative gives us the public world — Chancery, Dedlock, Bucket's relentless machinery of revelation.
And then there is the extraordinary portrait of Sir Leicester — a man reduced to a single dependency.
Dickens gives us this image — and I find it genuinely moving, despite everything —
"Sir Leicester Dedlock remains immovable, with the same icy surface upon him, except that he once or twice looks towards Mr. Bucket, as relying on that officer alone of all mankind."
That phrase — alone of all mankind — is one of the most desolate in the novel.
Here is the grandest man in England, and his whole world has narrowed to the face of a detective inspector.
The institution has crumbled, and the man — stripped bare — is more sympathetic than we ever thought he could be.
You've put your finger on something I've always felt when reading that passage — there's no contempt in it.
Dickens has been withering about Sir Leicester for hundreds of pages, and then in this crisis, he simply — stops.
He lets the man be human.
Which brings me — with some pleasure — to Mr. Turveydrop, who is never allowed to be human and who thoroughly deserves it.
Now here Dickens is at full comic stretch — the prose enacting the character's magnificent self-deception.
Listen to how he performs generosity —
"Do not even allow my simple requirements to be considered if they should at any time interfere with your own, my Caroline. Your necessities are greater than mine."
"Your necessities are greater than mine" — spoken, of course, by a man whose every necessity has been attended to for decades by his son.
The gap between the language and the reality — that's Dickens' comic genius in one sentence.
What I find extraordinary is that the comedy and the devastation run in parallel, right to the end.
Turveydrop flourishes; Richard dies; Esther gets her happy ending and can barely describe it without apologising for it.
That reticence in Esther — that inability to fully claim her own joy — is, I think, the novel's deepest wound.
Dickens gives her everything, and still she holds herself at arm's length from happiness.
Whether that's the novel's limitation or its most truthful insight about damaged people — I've never quite resolved it.
And perhaps that irresolution is exactly right for a novel called Bleak House.
I would put it slightly differently — and here I suspect we may have a small disagreement.
I don't read Esther's modesty as damage, precisely. I read it as a form of moral seriousness that the novel endorses.
She doesn't trumpet her goodness. She simply enacts it, page after page, without self-congratulation.
In an age that confused loudness with virtue — and our own is not so different — that is a considerable achievement.
The ending withholds, yes — but what it withholds is triumphalism. And that, I think, is wisdom.
Triumphalism withheld — that may be the finest gloss on this ending I've heard.
A novel that could so easily have been a denunciation or a celebration is, in the end, neither — it is a reckoning.
Sir Edmund, Oliver, Caroline — thank you for bringing such generosity and intelligence to this conversation.
Bleak House has outlasted every prediction of its own gloom — still surprising readers, still unresolved, still alive.
We hope you'll join us next time on Bleak House Unpacked.

c8:p24.text:
“Bleak House; true. There is, in that city of London there, some
property of ours which is much at this day what Bleak House was then;
I say property of ours, meaning of the suit’s, but I ought to call it
the property of costs, for costs is the only power on earth that will
ever get anything out of it now or will ever know it for anything but
an eyesore and a heartsore. It is a street of perishing blind houses,
with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much
as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their
hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of
rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and
every door might be death’s door) turning stagnant green, the very
crutches on which the ruins are propped decaying. Although Bleak
House was not in Chancery, its master was, and it was stamped with
the same seal. These are the Great Seal’s impressions, my dear, all
over England—the children know them!”
c8:p24.summary: Jarndyce describes a street of property nominally belonging to the Jarndyce suit but effectively owned by costs; the houses are in terrible decay, windowless, rusted, and desolate, bearing the Great Seal's mark of Chancery throughout England.
c8:p24.best_quote: It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and every door might be death's door) turning stagnant green

c42:p0.text:
From the verdant undulations and the spreading oaks of the Dedlock
property, Mr. Tulkinghorn transfers himself to the stale heat and
dust of London. His manner of coming and going between the two places
is one of his impenetrabilities. He walks into Chesney Wold as if it
were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he
had never been out of Lincoln’s Inn Fields. He neither changes his
dress before the journey nor talks of it afterwards. He melted out of
his turret-room this morning, just as now, in the late twilight, he
melts into his own square.
c42:p0.summary: Mr. Tulkinghorn returns from the Dedlock estate to his London chambers with characteristic mystery and detachment, indifferent to the journey and unchanged by it.
c42:p0.best_quote: He walks into Chesney Wold as if it were next door to his chambers and returns to his chambers as if he had never been out of Lincoln's Inn Fields.

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.
c6:p46.summary: Detailed description of Bleak House's furnishings in each room, establishing a warm, hospitable environment filled with quirky collections and careful comfort.
c6:p46.best_quote: with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House

c2:p4.text:
Sir Leicester Dedlock is only a baronet, but there is no mightier
baronet than he. His family is as old as the hills, and infinitely
more respectable. He has a general opinion that the world might get
on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks. He would on
the whole admit nature to be a good idea (a little low, perhaps, when
not enclosed with a park-fence), but an idea dependent for its
execution on your great county families. He is a gentleman of strict
conscience, disdainful of all littleness and meanness and ready on
the shortest notice to die any death you may please to mention rather
than give occasion for the least impeachment of his integrity. He is
an honourable, obstinate, truthful, high-spirited, intensely
prejudiced, perfectly unreasonable man.
c2:p4.summary: Sir Leicester Dedlock is a baronet of ancient family, rigid principles, and class-bound prejudices who views the social order as naturally ordained with his family at its apex.
c2:p4.best_quote: He has a general opinion that the world might get on without hills but would be done up without Dedlocks

c28:p37.text:
Sir Leicester is content enough that the ironmaster should feel that
there is no hurry there; there, in that ancient house, rooted in that
quiet park, where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and
the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the
fern and leaves of a hundred years; and where the sun-dial on the
terrace has dumbly recorded for centuries that time which was as much
the property of every Dedlock—while he lasted—as the house and
lands. Sir Leicester sits down in an easy-chair, opposing his repose
and that of Chesney Wold to the restless flights of ironmasters.
c28:p37.summary: Sir Leicester finds comfort in Chesney Wold's timelessness and repose, opposing it to the restless commercial flights of modern ironmasters.
c28:p37.best_quote: where the ivy and the moss have had time to mature, and the gnarled and warted elms and the umbrageous oaks stand deep in the fern and leaves of a hundred years

c9:p25.text:
“But it’s the inside of the man, the warm heart of the man, the
passion of the man, the fresh blood of the man, Rick—and Ada, and
little Cobweb too, for you are all interested in a visitor—that I
speak of,” he pursued. “His language is as sounding as his voice. He
is always in extremes, perpetually in the superlative degree. In his
condemnation he is all ferocity. You might suppose him to be an ogre
from what he says, and I believe he has the reputation of one with
some people. There! I tell you no more of him beforehand. You must
not be surprised to see him take me under his protection, for he has
never forgotten that I was a low boy at school and that our
friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant’s teeth out
(he says six) before breakfast. Boythorn and his man,” to me, “will
be here this afternoon, my dear.”
c9:p25.summary: Mr. Jarndyce explains Boythorn's passionate, extreme nature and his school friendship with him, rooted in Boythorn knocking out teeth of their tyrannical headmaster, setting expectations for his protective behavior.
c9:p25.best_quote: There! I tell you no more of him beforehand. You must not be surprised to see him take me under his protection, for he has never forgotten that I was a low boy at school and that our friendship began in his knocking two of my head tyrant's teeth out (he says six) before breakfast.

c51:p37.text:
Afterwards, when Mr. Woodcourt came to reflect on what had passed, he
was so very much impressed by the strength of Richard’s anxiety on
this point that in telling me generally of his first visit to
Symond’s Inn he particularly dwelt upon it. It revived a fear I had
had before that my dear girl’s little property would be absorbed by
Mr. Vholes and that Richard’s justification to himself would be
sincerely this. It was just as I began to take care of Caddy that the
interview took place, and I now return to the time when Caddy had
recovered and the shade was still between me and my darling.
c51:p37.summary: Esther reflects on Woodcourt's impression of Richard and her own fear that Ada's property will be consumed by the lawsuit, with Richard's concern for her being a sincere but compromising self-justification.
c51:p37.best_quote: It revived a fear I had had before that my dear girl's little property would be absorbed by Mr. Vholes and that Richard's justification to himself would be sincerely this.

c29:p1.text:
But the house in town, which is rarely in the same mind as Chesney
Wold at the same time, seldom rejoicing when it rejoices or mourning
when it mourns, excepting when a Dedlock dies—the house in town
shines out awakened. As warm and bright as so much state may be, as
delicately redolent of pleasant scents that bear no trace of winter
as hothouse flowers can make it, soft and hushed so that the ticking
of the clocks and the crisp burning of the fires alone disturb the
stillness in the rooms, it seems to wrap those chilled bones of Sir
Leicester’s in rainbow-coloured wool. And Sir Leicester is glad to
repose in dignified contentment before the great fire in the library,
condescendingly perusing the backs of his books or honouring the fine
arts with a glance of approbation. For he has his pictures, ancient
and modern. Some of the Fancy Ball School in which art occasionally
condescends to become a master, which would be best catalogued like
the miscellaneous articles in a sale. As “Three high-backed chairs, a
table and cover, long-necked bottle (containing wine), one flask, one
Spanish female’s costume, three-quarter face portrait of Miss Jogg
the model, and a suit of armour containing Don Quixote.” Or “One
stone terrace (cracked), one gondola in distance, one Venetian
senator’s dress complete, richly embroidered white satin costume with
profile portrait of Miss Jogg the model, one Scimitar superbly
mounted in gold with jewelled handle, elaborate Moorish dress (very
rare), and Othello.”
c29:p1.summary: The Dedlock townhouse is warm and bright, where Sir Leicester rests contentedly, examining his collection of art that Dickens satirizes as kitsch.

c2:p2.text:
My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days
previous to her departure for Paris, where her ladyship intends to
stay some weeks, after which her movements are uncertain. The
fashionable intelligence says so for the comfort of the Parisians,
and it knows all fashionable things. To know things otherwise were to
be unfashionable. My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in
familiar conversation, her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are
out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been
sapped and sopped away. The adjacent low-lying ground for half a mile
in breadth is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands in
it and a surface punctured all over, all day long, with falling rain.
My Lady Dedlock’s place has been extremely dreary. The weather for
many a day and night has been so wet that the trees seem wet through,
and the soft loppings and prunings of the woodman’s axe can make no
crash or crackle as they fall. The deer, looking soaked, leave
quagmires where they pass. The shot of a rifle loses its sharpness in
the moist air, and its smoke moves in a tardy little cloud towards
the green rise, coppice-topped, that makes a background for the
falling rain. The view from my Lady Dedlock’s own windows is
alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink. The vases
on the stone terrace in the foreground catch the rain all day; and
the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the broad flagged
pavement, called from old time the Ghost’s Walk, all night. On
Sundays the little church in the park is mouldy; the oaken pulpit
breaks out into a cold sweat; and there is a general smell and taste
as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady Dedlock (who is
childless), looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a
keeper’s lodge and seeing the light of a fire upon the latticed
panes, and smoke rising from the chimney, and a child, chased by a
woman, running out into the rain to meet the shining figure of a
wrapped-up man coming through the gate, has been put quite out of
temper. My Lady Dedlock says she has been “bored to death.”
c2:p2.summary: Lady Dedlock returns to her Lincolnshire estate before departing for Paris, where the landscape is depicted as relentlessly dreary and sodden; her observation of a family scene at a keeper's lodge disrupts her usual composure.
c2:p2.best_quote: The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
c12:p67.summary: At sunset, Tulkinghorn finally appears, moving at his usual methodical pace with an expressionless mask, embodying mystery and unknown knowledge.
c12:p67.best_quote: He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

c39:p87.text:
“A virtue in which few Englishmen are deficient,” observes Mr.
Tulkinghorn. He has been standing on the hearthstone with his back to
the smoked chimney-piece, and now turns round with his glasses to his
eyes. “Who is this? ‘Lady Dedlock.’ Ha! A very good likeness in its
way, but it wants force of character. Good day to you, gentlemen;
good day!”
c39:p87.summary: Tulkinghorn examines Lady Dedlock's portrait, comments cryptically on its weakness of character, and then takes his leave with a polite farewell.
c39:p87.best_quote: Who is this? 'Lady Dedlock.' Ha! A very good likeness in its way, but it wants force of character.

c48:p105.text:
For a little while they are silent. Lady Dedlock has eaten no dinner,
but has twice or thrice poured out water with a steady hand and drunk
it. She rises from table, takes a lounging-chair, and reclines in it,
shading her face. There is nothing in her manner to express weakness
or excite compassion. It is thoughtful, gloomy, concentrated. “This
woman,” thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark
object closing up her view, “is a study.”
c48:p105.summary: In the silence that follows, Lady Dedlock maintains thoughtful composure while remaining emotionally turbulent; Tulkinghorn regards her as a fascinating psychological study.
c48:p105.best_quote: This woman,' thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, 'is a study.'

c36:p18.text:
I was resting at my favourite point after a long ramble, and Charley
was gathering violets at a little distance from me. I had been
looking at the Ghost’s Walk lying in a deep shade of masonry afar off
and picturing to myself the female shape that was said to haunt it
when I became aware of a figure approaching through the wood. The
perspective was so long and so darkened by leaves, and the shadows of
the branches on the ground made it so much more intricate to the eye,
that at first I could not discern what figure it was. By little and
little it revealed itself to be a woman’s—a lady’s—Lady Dedlock’s.
She was alone and coming to where I sat with a much quicker step, I
observed to my surprise, than was usual with her.
c36:p18.summary: As Esther rests at her favorite spot, a woman emerges through the wood—Lady Dedlock, approaching with unusual haste and emotion.

c43:p80.text:
“It has given me pain, Mr. Jarndyce,” Sir Leicester weightily
proceeded. “I assure you, sir, it has given—me—pain—to learn from
the housekeeper at Chesney Wold that a gentleman who was in your
company in that part of the county, and who would appear to possess a
cultivated taste for the fine arts, was likewise deterred by some
such cause from examining the family pictures with that leisure, that
attention, that care, which he might have desired to bestow upon them
and which some of them might possibly have repaid.” Here he produced
a card and read, with much gravity and a little trouble, through his
eye-glass, “Mr. Hirrold—Herald—Harold—Skampling—Skumpling—I beg
your pardon—Skimpole.”
c43:p80.summary: Sir Leicester reports that Skimpole, when visiting Lincolnshire, was also deterred from viewing Chesney Wold's pictures, which gave him pain to learn.
c43:p80.best_quote: I assure you, sir, it has given—me—pain—to learn from the housekeeper at Chesney Wold that a gentleman who was in your company in that part of the county, and who would appear to possess a cultivated taste for the fine arts, was likewise deterred by some such cause from examining the family pictures with that leisure, that attention, that care, which he might have desired to bestow upon them.

c51:p21.text:
“Woodcourt, my dear fellow,” cried Richard, starting up with extended
hands, “you come upon my vision like a ghost.”
c51:p21.summary: Richard enthusiastically welcomes Woodcourt, comparing his sudden appearance to a ghostly visitation.
c51:p21.best_quote: you come upon my vision like a ghost

c45:p72.text:
“Her gratitude to you, Mr. Woodcourt, is delightful. She is a most
affectionate creature, as I have reason to say.”
c45:p72.summary: Esther remarks on Miss Flite's affection and gratitude toward Woodcourt.

c60:p24.text:
“So he tells me,” returned my guardian. “Very good. He has made his
protest, and Dame Durden has made hers, and there is nothing more to
be said about it. Now I come to Mrs. Woodcourt. How do you like her,
my dear?”
c60:p24.summary: Jarndyce accepts that Esther and Woodcourt have already discussed it with Richard and shifts to asking Esther's opinion of Mrs. Woodcourt.

c39:p58.text:
Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus’ purse
of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.
Regularly, every morning at eight, is the elder Mr. Smallweed brought
down to the corner and carried in, accompanied by Mrs. Smallweed,
Judy, and Bart; and regularly, all day, do they all remain there
until nine at night, solaced by gipsy dinners, not abundant in
quantity, from the cook’s shop, rummaging and searching, digging,
delving, and diving among the treasures of the late lamented. What
those treasures are they keep so secret that the court is maddened.
In its delirium it imagines guineas pouring out of tea-pots,
crown-pieces overflowing punch-bowls, old chairs and mattresses
stuffed with Bank of England notes. It possesses itself of the
sixpenny history (with highly coloured folding frontispiece) of Mr.
Daniel Dancer and his sister, and also of Mr. Elwes, of Suffolk, and
transfers all the facts from those authentic narratives to Mr. Krook.
Twice when the dustman is called in to carry off a cartload of old
paper, ashes, and broken bottles, the whole court assembles and pries
into the baskets as they come forth. Many times the two gentlemen who
write with the ravenous little pens on the tissue-paper are seen
prowling in the neighbourhood—shy of each other, their late
partnership being dissolved. The Sol skilfully carries a vein of the
prevailing interest through the Harmonic nights. Little Swills, in
what are professionally known as “patter” allusions to the subject,
is received with loud applause; and the same vocalist “gags” in the
regular business like a man inspired. Even Miss M. Melvilleson, in
the revived Caledonian melody of “We’re a-Nodding,” points the
sentiment that “the dogs love broo” (whatever the nature of that
refreshment may be) with such archness and such a turn of the head
towards next door that she is immediately understood to mean Mr.
Smallweed loves to find money, and is nightly honoured with a double
encore. For all this, the court discovers nothing; and as Mrs. Piper
and Mrs. Perkins now communicate to the late lodger whose appearance
is the signal for a general rally, it is in one continual ferment to
discover everything, and more.
c39:p58.summary: The entire court becomes obsessed with Smallweed's search through Krook's possessions, inventing elaborate fantasies about hidden treasure. The narrator describes daily routines and even entertainment at the local pub incorporating references to the search.
c39:p58.best_quote: Never since it has been a court has it had such a Fortunatus' purse of gossip as in the proceedings at the rag and bottle shop.

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c31:p92.text:
He was extremely gay all the rest of the evening, for he absolutely
chirped—those were his delighted words—when he thought by what a
happy talent for business he was surrounded. He gave us, in his glass
of negus, “Better health to our young friend!” and supposed and gaily
pursued the case of his being reserved like Whittington to become
Lord Mayor of London. In that event, no doubt, he would establish the
Jarndyce Institution and the Summerson Almshouses, and a little
annual Corporation Pilgrimage to St. Albans. He had no doubt, he
said, that our young friend was an excellent boy in his way, but his
way was not the Harold Skimpole way; what Harold Skimpole was, Harold
Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he
first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his
failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the
bargain; and he hoped we would do the same.
c31:p92.summary: Skimpole cheerfully pursues fanciful thoughts about Jo becoming Lord Mayor, then expounds his philosophy of self-acceptance without moral growth.
c31:p92.best_quote: what Harold Skimpole was, Harold Skimpole had found himself, to his considerable surprise, when he first made his own acquaintance; he had accepted himself with all his failings and had thought it sound philosophy to make the best of the bargain

c5:p86.text:
When I told him, he laughed. In the same odd way, yet with the same
rapidity, he then produced singly, and rubbed out singly, the letters
forming the words Bleak House. These, in some astonishment, I also
read; and he laughed again.
c5:p86.summary: Esther reads both 'Jarndyce' and 'Bleak House' with astonishment; Krook laughs mysteriously.

c47:p105.text:
Phil Squod, with his smoky gunpowder visage, at once acts as nurse
and works as armourer at his little table in a corner, often looking
